opus-5.5.text:
Sure. I'd say KDA is really an incremental step on a line of work that's been developing for a few years. It isn't a sudden invention.

The starting point is linear attention. You compress the whole history into a fixed-size state, basically a matrix, instead of keeping an ever-growing KV cache. The original linear attention just keeps adding key-value outer products into that state, so it gets cluttered. It has no good way to forget or overwrite things.

The delta rule fixes the overwriting part. Before you write a new key-value pair, you first read out what the state currently associates with that key, then write in only the correction, the "delta." You can think of it as one step of online gradient descent on a regression loss. The memory is actively trying to store the right value for each key, rather than blindly accumulating. That's DeltaNet.

Then there's forgetting. Mamba2-style models use a decay gate, so old information fades away. Gated DeltaNet combines the two: the delta rule for precise, targeted updates, and a gate for global forgetting. These two mechanisms turned out to be complementary.

KDA's main change is to make the gate much finer-grained. In Gated DeltaNet, the decay is essentially a scalar per head, so the whole memory matrix fades at the same rate. In KDA the gate is channel-wise. Different dimensions of the state can forget at different speeds. Some channels can hold long-term information, others can turn over quickly. That gives the model much more expressive control over its memory, a bit like what GLA did compared to scalar-gated linear attention.

The difficulty is always efficiency. Finer-grained gating can easily ruin the hardware-friendly chunkwise parallel algorithm. So a lot of the design work was about structuring the transition matrix, a constrained diagonal-plus-low-rank form, so that you keep the expressiveness but can still train it in parallel with matmul-heavy kernels on GPUs. That's a recurring philosophy for me: an architecture only matters if it can be trained efficiently at scale.

Finally, KDA isn't meant to replace attention entirely. In Kimi Linear it's used in a hybrid, with most layers being KDA and a fraction being full global attention. The linear layers handle most of the computation cheaply and give the model a strong sense of local and positional structure. The few full-attention layers provide the exact retrieval that a fixed-size state fundamentally can't. So the design logic is: make the recurrent memory as expressive as possible while keeping it hardware-efficient, then let a small amount of full attention cover what compression can't.

r001.rationale: The response presents KDA as building on Gated DeltaNet’s delta updates while adding channel-wise gating, and compares that finer-grained gating to GLA.

r002.rationale: It says Gated DeltaNet uses a scalar-per-head decay, then explains that finer-grained gating can undermine the hardware-friendly chunkwise algorithm, connecting the coarser decay to efficiency.

r003.rationale: The response describes KDA’s efficiency challenges and design, but does not say that later implementation advances made fine-grained decay worth reconsidering.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. I think the cleanest way to understand KDA is to see it as the point where two lines of work I've been involved in finally meet. One line is gating, the other is the delta rule, and for a long time they were developed somewhat separately.

Let me start with the delta rule, because that's the heart of it. If you look at vanilla linear attention, the state update is just an outer product: you take the key and value, multiply them, and add that to the memory matrix. That's a pure write. Nothing ever gets erased except through decay. The delta rule changes this into something closer to an online learning step. Before you write a new value, you first read what the memory currently predicts for that key, compute the error between the prediction and the actual value, and then you only write the error. So it's a correction, not an accumulation. If you think about it from the test-time regression view, the memory is a linear model, the keys and values are the training pairs, and each token is one step of gradient descent on a squared loss. That framing matters because it tells you the recurrence is doing something principled. It isn't just a kernel trick for softmax attention anymore. It's solving an associative recall problem, and in practice that's where vanilla linear attention and Mamba-style models struggle most.

Now, the gating side. In Gated DeltaNet we added a decay term on top of the delta rule, but it was a scalar per head. One number controls how fast the entire head forgets. That's convenient for the chunkwise algorithm, but it's a pretty blunt instrument. In GLA, the earlier work, we had a fine-grained gate, a diagonal matrix, so every channel of the state could have its own forgetting rate. The intuition there is that different feature dimensions carry information at different timescales. Some channels should behave like a short-term buffer, some should hold onto things for a very long time. And in a model with no positional encoding, which is what Kimi Linear does on the global attention layers, that channel-wise decay is effectively your positional signal. The decay pattern itself encodes relative position.

So KDA is simply: fine-grained channel-wise gating from GLA, combined with the delta rule from DeltaNet. Mathematically the transition matrix becomes diagonal plus a rank-one term, where the diagonal is the per-channel decay and the rank-one part is the delta correction. That family, diagonal plus low rank, has been explored in general form, but the general form is expensive and also numerically fragile when you train at scale. The real work in KDA is constraining the structure so that the chunkwise algorithm still works. You need to be able to express a chunk of updates in a compact form, something like the WY representation for products of Householder-like matrices, and the fine-grained decay complicates that because now you're tracking cumulative decays per channel inside the chunk. We found a parameterization where you can still do it, and it ends up with noticeably less computation than the general DPLR version. The gate itself is also kept cheap, basically a low-rank projection, so the parameter cost is small.

The last part of the design logic is that KDA isn't meant to live alone. It's hybridized with full attention, roughly three linear layers for every one global attention layer. My view has always been that linear attention should take over the workload where it's good, the local and medium-range modeling and the bulk of the KV cache cost, and leave the truly global retrieval to a small number of softmax layers. The point of making KDA stronger per layer is that it lets you push that ratio further while matching or beating a full attention baseline at the same compute, and then the decoding speedup at long context just comes for free, because the state is constant size.

So if I compress it: delta rule gives you precise write and erase, fine-grained gating gives you multi-timescale memory and replaces position encoding, and the hardware-aware constraints are what make the combination actually trainable at scale rather than a nice equation on paper.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly combines GLA’s fine-grained channel-wise gating with the delta rule from DeltaNet.

r002.rationale: It says Gated DeltaNet used scalar per-head decay because it was convenient for the chunkwise algorithm, tying the coarser decay to implementation efficiency.

r003.rationale: It describes a parameterization that makes fine-grained decay work with chunkwise updates and reduces computation compared with general DPLR, explaining why it became practical to revisit.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a question of what a model should remember, and how it should revise that memory. Attention design is partly about balancing the cost of preserving information with the ability to retrieve the right information later.

For KDA specifically, though, we haven’t introduced its mechanism yet, so I’d be careful about attributing a particular design rationale to it. The questions I’d use to understand it are: What information does it retain? How does new information update or replace what’s already there? And what does that trade off in efficiency and retrieval accuracy? Those are the connections I’d want to establish before explaining why its design works.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify KDA as combining Gated Linear Attention and Gated DeltaNet; it only raises general questions about memory and attention.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Gated DeltaNet, coarser-grained decay, or efficiency constraints.

r003.rationale: It does not mention implementation advances or explain why fine-grained decay in gated attention became worth reconsidering.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d understand KDA as an attempt to make linear attention’s memory more selective: what should the model keep, what should it forget, and how should it correct what it has already stored?

In ordinary attention, you retain the past keys and values and retrieve from them directly. Linear attention instead compresses that history into a fixed-size state, which is efficient, but makes the quality of memory updates especially important.

The delta-rule idea is to make each write a correction. You first ask what the current memory would return for a key, compare that with the incoming value, and then write the difference. That helps avoid repeatedly accumulating information the memory already represents.

KDA combines that corrective update with fine-grained gating. Different parts of the memory can decay at different rates, so the model has more control over retaining useful information while replacing information that has become irrelevant.

So the design logic is selective forgetting plus corrective writing, within an architecture that remains efficient to execute. The central tradeoff is how much of attention’s retrieval quality you can preserve while compressing the history into a bounded memory.

r003.rationale: It does not mention later implementation advances or explain that they prompted reconsideration of fine-grained decay in gated attention.
